raw_text:
# Cardiac Contractility Modulation Therapy in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction
Heart failure (HF) remains a significant global health burden, characterized by high morbidity, frequent hospitalizations, and poor quality of life despite advanced pharmacotherapies [1]. While cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) has revolutionized device-based management for patients with a wide QRS complex (typically $\ge 120\text{--}130\text{ ms}$), a large subset of symptomatic patients present with a narrow QRS duration and are therefore ineligible for biventricular pacing [2,3]. For these patients, cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) has emerged as an innovative, device-based therapy designed to bridge this therapeutic gap [1]. Current international guidelines from the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) [2] and the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) [3] recognize CCM as a potential therapeutic option for selected symptomatic patients with HF.

## Mechanisms of Action
The physiological rationale behind CCM relies on the delivery of non-excitatory, high-voltage biphasic electrical signals to the right ventricular septum during the absolute refractory period of the action potential [4]. Unlike pacing or defibrillation, these signals do not trigger new contractions, nor do they alter the electrical activation sequence [4,5]. At the cellular level, CCM has been shown in animal models to acutely increase intracellular calcium transients, enhancing sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium loading and restoring the function of key calcium-handling proteins like SERCA2a and phospholamban [6]. Critically, unlike classic positive inotropes, this enhancement in contractile force occurs without an increase in myocardial oxygen consumption [7] or alterations in global myocardial efficiency [8]. Long-term delivery of CCM therapy has been associated with reverse molecular remodeling, including a reversion of the maladaptive fetal gene expression program characteristic of chronic HF back toward normal physiological states [9].

## Clinical Trial Evidence
The clinical efficacy and safety of CCM have been established through a series of randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Early feasibility trials, such as the European FIX-HF-4 [10] and the US-based FIX-HF-5 [11] trials, demonstrated that CCM was safe and could significantly improve exercise tolerance and quality of life. Subgroup analyses of these early cohorts revealed that patients with a moderately reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF 25%–45%) derived the greatest benefit [12].

This finding paved the way for the pivotal FIX-HF-5C confirmatory trial, which randomized 160 patients with NYHA class III/IV symptoms, narrow QRS complexes, and LVEF between 25% and 45% to CCM plus guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) versus GDMT alone [13]. At 24 weeks, CCM therapy demonstrated statistically significant improvements in peak oxygen consumption ($\text{peak } \mathrm{VO_2}$), 6-minute walk distance, and health-related quality of life, alongside a reduction in the composite of cardiovascular death and HF-related hospitalizations [13]. The follow-up FIX-HF-5C2 trial evaluated a streamlined two-lead Optimizer system (eliminating the right atrial lead), confirming equivalent safety and efficacy with fewer lead-related complications [14]. Meta-analyses of these clinical trials have consistently demonstrated the reproducible benefits of CCM on functional capacity and clinical symptoms [15,16].

## Long-Term and Real-World Evidence
While randomized trials provide high-quality short-term data, real-world registries have shed light on the long-term safety and survival benefits of CCM. The European CCM-REG registry, which tracked real-world cohorts, demonstrated that the functional improvements in NYHA class and quality of life are sustained for up to two years post-implantation, accompanied by a significant (>70%) reduction in HF-related hospitalization rates [17,18]. Longitudinal and observational single-center studies have also suggested a signal toward improved long-term survival compared with predictions based on conventional risk-scoring models [19,20]. Furthermore, real-world data have clarified technical questions: trials comparing single- versus dual-ventricular lead delivery showed similar safety and efficacy profiles [21].

## Patient Selection and Future Perspectives
Appropriate patient selection remains key to maximizing the clinical response of CCM. In clinical practice, CCM has been effectively applied to patients who are non-responders to biventricular pacing (CRT) [22,23], as well as across different etiologies of heart failure. For instance, data from the MAINTAINED registry demonstrated that while patients with non-ischemic cardiomyopathy may achieve greater improvements in LVEF, those with ischemic cardiomyopathy also derive significant long-term clinical benefits [24].

An exciting avenue of research is the expansion of CCM beyond patients with reduced ejection fraction. The pilot CCM-HFpEF study demonstrated that CCM therapy is safe and improves health status in patients with heart failure and preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), a population with historically limited device-based options [25]. Current comprehensive reviews [26,27] and expert consensus pathways [28] continue to outline the practical candidate profile, emphasizing the utility of CCM as a complementary treatment option alongside medical therapy and invasive hemodynamics monitoring [29]. Longitudinal analyses also indicate that baseline LVEF does not restrict long-term survival benefit, confirming its broad applicability [30].

## Conclusion
Cardiac contractility modulation represents a validated, device-based approach that safely improves exercise capacity, quality of life, and clinical outcomes in symptomatic heart failure patients ineligible for CRT. Future studies, including those combining CCM with implantable cardioverter-defibrillator platforms and larger HFpEF cohorts, will further solidify its role in the contemporary heart failure management paradigm.
